title: Smallest dimension of a cubic-homogeneous Jacobian counterexample
W: The Jacobian conjecture is now known to fail. A classical reduction says that if it fails at all, it fails for maps of the special form x + (cubic homogeneous terms), but the reduction pays for this by raising the number of variables. Such a cubic counterexample is now known in 18 variables, and none exists in 4 or fewer. What is the smallest number of variables in which one exists?
M: Let $N_3$ be the least $n$ such that there is $H=(H_1,\dots,H_n)$, each $H_i\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ homogeneous of degree 3, with $JH$ nilpotent (equivalently $\det(I+JH)=1$) and $x+H$ not an automorphism of $\mathbb C^n$. By Hubbers' classification (JC holds for cubic homogeneous maps with $n\le4$), $N_3\ge5$; the stabilization of Alp\"oge's map in arXiv:2610.24889 gives $N_3\le18$ (unrefereed). Determine $N_3$. Companion: determine $d_3$, the least polynomial degree of a non-invertible Keller map $\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ (known $3\le d_3\le7$).
why: The Bass-Connell-Wright/Yagzhev reduction to cubic homogeneous maps (and Druzkowski's to cubic-linear) organized forty years of work on the Jacobian conjecture: small-n classifications of nilpotent cubic Jacobians (Hubbers, de Bondt, van den Essen), quasi-translations, Zhao's vanishing conjecture. With the conjecture refuted, N_3 is the canonical measure of where that whole structural program actually breaks, and it is testable against the existing classification machinery from below and explicit constructions from above.
diagnosis: B because the minimal degree in dimension 3 is one numeric invariant of one dimension; the reviewer noted the newer families might already lower it. The canonical boundary is the one in the cubic-homogeneous normal form that the field was built around.
what_changed: Replaced 'minimal degree in dimension 3' by the minimal dimension of a cubic-homogeneous counterexample (the reduction's canonical form), with explicit bounds 5<=N_3<=18; kept d_3 as a companion. Status of n=5 (de Bondt) not verified.

title: Blow-up under a steady force
W: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a push that varies in time and is switched on and off. Can a smooth, compactly supported push that never changes in time also drive a fluid at rest to a singularity?
M:
Decide whether there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, independent of $t$, such that the solution of $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=\Delta u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ loses smoothness in finite time.
why: Steady stirring is the physically basic forcing, and a time-independent force cannot be tuned to the scales of a developing singularity. A positive answer would mean the singularity is produced by the nonlinearity alone under a fixed energy input. A negative answer would show that the time-dependent forcing in known constructions is essential.
diagnosis: Natural, but essentially Millennium-level difficulty (steady forcing is subcritical at small scales, so blow-up is effectively unforced); the time-dependent forced result it builds on is unrefereed. Every natural variant is famous-adjacent or harder.

title: Positive metric entropy for the x^4+y^4 billiard
W: The billiard table x^4 + y^4 <= 1 is smooth and convex, but its curvature vanishes at four points, so (by Mather) it has no caustics. Its phase space mixes stable islands with apparently chaotic regions. Prove that the chaos is real: on a set of positive measure, nearby trajectories separate exponentially fast.
M:
Let $\Phi$ be the billiard map of $\Omega=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$, preserving the Liouville measure $
u=\sin	heta\,ds\,d	heta$. Prove that $h_
u(\Phi)>0$; equivalently, by Pesin's formula, that $\Phi$ has a nonzero Lyapunov exponent on a set of positive $
u$-measure.
why: Proving positive metric entropy for any smooth, area-preserving twist map with coexisting KAM islands, such as the Chirikov standard map, is a central and notoriously hard open problem. No smooth (C^2 or better) convex billiard is known to have positive metric entropy: the known examples, like stadiums and lemons, have boundary singularities. The analytic table x^4 + y^4 = 1 is the most natural concrete test case, and numerics show entropy of about 0.65 there.
diagnosis: Instance of a listed open problem: Bunimovich's survey (Problem 2) asks to construct a strictly convex C^1 / convex C^2 table with positive metric entropy. Knill already studied the l^p family numerically. The general version is famous; this instance is not novel.

title: Mean-zero weights shift the Fujita exponent
W: Fujita's theorem says that for u_t = Δu + u^p in d dimensions, every positive solution blows up when p ≤ 1+2/d, and small solutions survive when p is larger. Replace u^p by a(x)u^p, where a is periodic and averages to zero. The first-order effect cancels, and a homogenization heuristic predicts an effective term proportional to u^(2p-1), which would move the threshold to p = 1+1/d. Prove that this is the true threshold.
M: Let $d\ge1$, $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^d)$ with $\int_{\mathbb T^d}a=0$, $a\not\equiv0$, viewed as a $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic function on $\mathbb R^d$. Consider $u_t=\Delta u+a(x)u^p$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$, $u_0\ge0$, $u_0\not\equiv0$. Prove: (i) if $1<p\le 1+1/d$, every such solution blows up in finite time; (ii) if $p>1+1/d$, solutions with sufficiently small $u_0$ are global. The critical case $d=1$, $p=2$, $a=\cos x$ (every positive solution of $u_t=u_{xx}+\cos(x)u^2$ blows up) is the test case.
why: Fujita thresholds are among the most studied phenomena in nonlinear parabolic PDE, and all known weighted versions (Pinsky; Meier; degenerate and potential variants) use weights with a sign, where the threshold is set by scaling. A mean-zero oscillating weight is the cleanest case where the leading effect cancels and the threshold is produced by a nonlinear second-order homogenization correction (constant c = <a,(-Δ)^{-1}a> > 0, effective v_t = Δv + c p v^(2p-1)). Proving it requires controlling homogenization over infinite time windows at criticality, which current test-function and Kaplan methods cannot do because the weight changes sign.
diagnosis: B for being one specific equation (cos x, d=1, p=2) and an uncertain literature check. The real content is the structural claim that zero-mean oscillation halves the Fujita excess, from 2/d to 1/d.
what_changed: Promoted the general-d, general-p threshold p*=1+1/d to the main statement, with cos-weight d=1 critical case as test case. Additional searches found no treatment of mean-zero periodic weights.

title: Outer billiards around analytic tables with flat points
W: Outer billiards around a smooth convex shape with positive curvature has only bounded orbits (Moser-Douady). Polygons, semicircles and generic C^1 shapes can have orbits that escape to infinity. What if the table is analytic and strictly convex, but its curvature vanishes at a few points, like the superellipse x^4+y^4 ≤ 1? Decide whether every orbit stays bounded.
M: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a strictly convex body whose boundary is a real-analytic curve, with curvature vanishing at finitely many points. Let $T(p)=2q-p$ be the outer billiard map, where $q\in\partial K$ is the tangency point of the right-hand tangent from $p$. Decide whether every $T$-orbit is bounded for all such $K$. If not, decide whether boundedness depends on the vanishing orders. The first test case is $K=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$.
why: Moser's question about which tables confine all orbits now has sharp answers at both extremes: Douady's positive-curvature C^6 theorem, and C^1-generic escape (2026), which relies on a purely singular radius-of-curvature measure. Analytic tables with isolated flat points sit in between. The boundary is as smooth as possible, but the radius of curvature has integrable singularities ~|θ|^{-k/(k+1)} at a point of curvature vanishing order k (|θ|^{-2/3} for x^4+y^4), so the twist map at infinity is only Hölder and KAM does not apply. This isolates curvature degeneracy, rather than lack of smoothness, as the possible cause of escape.
diagnosis: B because x^4+y^4 is one arbitrary instance. The canonical question is the class: analytic strictly convex tables with isolated zero-curvature points. Neither the generic C^1 result nor Douady's theorem covers it, and I found nothing that treats it.
what_changed: Generalized from the single superellipse to all analytic strictly convex tables with finitely many flat points, and asked whether boundedness depends on the vanishing order. Kept x^4+y^4 as the test case.

title: Infinitely many knot types in the symmetric ABC flow
W: Steady Euler flows can carry knotted streamlines, and generic high-frequency Beltrami fields on the torus contain every knot. Show that the most-studied explicit example, the ABC flow with A = B = C = 1, has closed streamlines tied in infinitely many different knots.
M: Let $X=(\sin z+\cos y,\ \sin x+\cos z,\ \sin y+\cos x)$ on $\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ (a curl eigenfield, $\nabla\times X=X$). Prove that the periodic orbits of $X$ that lie in some embedded 3-ball $B\subset\mathbb T^3$ realize infinitely many distinct knot types (as knots in $B\cong$ a ball in $\mathbb R^3$). Stronger: every knot type is realized.
why: The ABC flow with A=B=C=1 is the standard model of Lagrangian chaos in steady Euler flows and of fast-dynamo theory, yet rigorous results on its dynamics are mostly perturbative (near integrable parameters) or about non-contractible orbits. Etnyre–Ghrist and Enciso–Peralta-Salas proved that some steady Euler or Beltrami flows realize all knots, using perturbations or random high-frequency fields. Proving it for this explicit lowest-frequency field would most likely need a computer-assisted horseshoe plus template theory (Birman–Williams), turning numerical evidence of chaos into topological information.
diagnosis: One explicit field, and the problem is a computer-assisted horseshoe plus template computation. Its general versions (all knots in some Beltrami / Euler flows) are already theorems (Etnyre-Ghrist, Enciso-Peralta-Salas). A hard technical target, but conceptually incremental.

title: Geodesic squares on convex surfaces
W: On a smooth convex surface, measure distance by the length of the shortest path on the surface. Every smooth simple closed curve on the surface should contain four points that form a 'square' in this sense: four equal sides and two equal diagonals.
M: Let $S=\partial K$ for a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ with smooth boundary and positive Gaussian curvature, and let $d$ be the intrinsic distance on $S$. Prove that every smooth simple closed curve $\gamma\subset S$ contains four distinct points $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, in this cyclic order along $\gamma$, with $d(p_1,p_2)=d(p_2,p_3)=d(p_3,p_4)=d(p_4,p_1)>0$ and $d(p_1,p_3)=d(p_2,p_4)$.
why: This is the Toeplitz square peg problem moved from the plane to intrinsic geometry. In the plane the smooth case is classical (Schnirelmann), and there are strong recent results (Greene-Lobb rectangles). Recent work extends inscription theorems to constant-curvature surfaces: the hyperbolic plane, and spheres for curves disjoint from their antipodal image. A general convex surface tests whether the topological parity argument survives variable curvature and a non-smooth distance function (cut loci).
diagnosis: The square version on convex surfaces is likely true by adapting the parity argument. The natural generalization, inscription for null-homotopic curves on surfaces of variable or nonpositive curvature, is already posed as an open question in arXiv:2507.07945, so it is not novel.

title: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
W: A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, without hitting edges or corners, traces a closed polygon in space. Is any such polygon knotted, and do infinitely many different knot types occur?
M: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of $T$ and its image is an embedded closed polygon. (a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite.
why: In the cube, periodic billiard trajectories are exactly the Lissajous knots (Jones-Przytycki), and infinitely many knot types occur because the cube unfolds to a lattice. The regular tetrahedron does not tile space and its dihedral angle arccos(1/3) is an irrational multiple of pi, so its unfolding group is not discrete. Even the existence of periodic orbits in tetrahedra is subtle, and knot types are an untouched invariant here.
diagnosis: Niche problem. Koseleff-Pecker showed that every knot is a billiard knot in some convex prism, so the general 'which knots are billiard knots' question is largely settled. The tetrahedron is canonical, but this remains a single-domain question of modest interest.

title: Fibonacci-modulated growing Jacobi matrix
W: Take a Jacobi matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal weights sqrt(n). Double the weight at every position where the Fibonacci word has a 1. Periodic modulations of power-growing weights are known to produce spectral phase transitions. Determine the spectral type for this aperiodic modulation.
M: Let $f=f_1f_2f_3\cdots=0100101001001\cdots\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ be the Fibonacci word, the fixed point of $0\mapsto01,\ 1\mapsto0$. Let $J$ be the Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with $(Ju)_n=a_{n-1}u_{n-1}+a_nu_{n+1}$, where $a_n=\sqrt n\,(1+f_n)$ and $a_0u_0:=0$. Since $\sum 1/a_n=\infty$, $J$ is self-adjoint (Carleman). Determine the spectral type of $J$. In particular: is $\sigma_{ac}(J)\neq\emptyset$? Is $\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$? Is the spectrum on some interval pure point or singular continuous?
why: Janas, Naboko, Swiderski and others classified unbounded Jacobi matrices with periodically modulated power-growing weights. Whether the spectrum is absolutely continuous, a gap, or point spectrum is decided by the trace of a single period's transfer matrix. A Fibonacci modulation joins this theory to the trace-map dynamics of quasicrystal Schrodinger operators. In that setting the period matrix is replaced by a hierarchy of block products.
diagnosis: The exponent 1/2 and the factor 2 are arbitrary. The general family (substitution-modulated power-growing weights) is a reasonable extension of Janas-Naboko-Swiderski theory, but it remains a niche spectral-theory question rather than A-level.
